  • #Physlib > Pull request checklists

Another idea (suggested before):

I think we should automate a short message on new PRs saying:

  • Review process will most likely involve some back and forth.
  • Feel free to put a message on #Physlib > PR reviews to draw attention to a PR.
  • If you use AI, please declare how.

Speaking from the peanut gallery: obviously mathlib's AI policy does not apply to physlib directly --- but you're of course welcome to borrow liberally from it, adopt it wholesale (or ask me to explain some of the trade-offs to you, e.g. in a brief video call).

Many thanks @Michael Rothgang ! I might take you up on this offer of a brief video call - not least because I'm interested on your view on how these sorts of things would scale (down) to projects like Physlib.

One bit of infrastructure that I was thinking of (mentioned to some in private) is an easy way to link to other implementation of results outside of Physlib, with something like: 

other_implementation "link_to_code_on_gitHub/reference" "Description of the implementation and how it is different"

This can then be used to find other implementations (maybe even private ones?), so that it is easier to understand what else has been done and where.
(As an example I made this PR Physlib#1111, which adds the meta program and a link to one of @Tyler Josephson ⚛️ 's groups codebase)
This sounds like a great idea. I’ve seen references like this previously in comments, but links would be better.
Yeah - hopefully the idea is that using something like this it will be easier to search and collate these sorts of things.
Another infrastructure idea: labels for different levels of AI contribution similar to here. Idea stolen from #general > PSA: mathlib AI policy @ 💬

As discussed in the PR review meet about the domain expertise needed for the review, will it be good to have a reviewer recommendation for each PR? based on the contributors who have worked on nearest folder, most active/recent contributors or those who have written or used the underlying API being called in the code under review? The PR request can then be sent to the contributors and if they decline, to the next most suitable contributor etc

Gitlab even has this as a feature: https://about.gitlab.com/blog/gitlab-suggested-reviewers/ (surfaced during search for similar ideas, dont know if this is actually used by anyone)

I'm not sure if this is a big problem worth the time implementing the solution, but thought to ask since the issue was mentioned in meet

I think Mathlib has a system like this, where reviewers are pinged (or at least I recall such a system being talked about before). I think even a low-tech system would work, in which people who want to review just declare what areas they are happy to review, and the system works based on that information.

I think this is probably worth spending time on, given I think efficient reviews are important to the success of projects like this. If this could be made into a GitHub workflow this would be good, as this wouldn't rely on an external server (which costs money).
I will look into it then, will also look into how mathlib is doing it.
For Mathlib there is a bot called mathlib-triage which assigns reviews to people (see e.g.) #36922

Been reading how codebases in general handle PR allocation (Codeowners) and mathilb in particular (Section 7 of Baanen et al., Growing Mathlib: maintenance of a large scale mathematical library is on review process).

I would divide this problem in two parts: any PR allocation assistant must involve two layers:

  1. Layer1: building a mapping of contributors and their domain - folder, file and definition/proof level. This layer can serve other purposes as well - any new member can directly see which contributor to talk to for their domain/data structure of interest

  2. Layer2: the PR assignment based on the mapping in layer1 - a github action to be triggered whenever a PR is made, would like to following features - figure out which metrics to be used (proximity to files, similarity of the definitions etc) to rank the candidates to be pinged, ping them, allow them to accept/reject etc.
I think these two layers sound good.

Read page 11-17 from mathlib paper in detail and it exactly provides with the prescriptive and procedural guidelines on how mathlib addresses technical debt and scaling code review, will study these in details over next few days and implement scaffolding on PhysLib :

Procedural:

  1. A technical-debt metric calculation on each PR: https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib-ci/blob/master/scripts/reporting/technical-debt-metrics.sh
  2. An automated PR summary comment generator for each PR
  3. PR to Zulip integration
  4. PR review guide: https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/pr-review.html
  5. PR Dashboard: https://leanprover-community.github.io/queueboard/index.html
  6. A reviewer map file collecting each reviewer's area of interest and expertise

Prescriptive:

  1. Maintainers should cover breadth of topics
  2. Each topic should have multiple knowledgeable maintainers to take difficult decisions
  3. The mathlib automations ensure 1/3 of merged PRs are actually given green light by reviewers
  4. Live review sessions
  5. Created custom python and shell scripts instead of relying on github exposed metrics and workflows
  6. Dashboard should be usable by maintainers, reviewers and contributors

I find some of the bullets in the previous comment hard to parse. I'm not sure if all of these match the original paper (which I co-authored). Let me clarify that

  • (3) seems off: every PR in mathlib needs to be approved by a maintainer (who can then decide to merge it). Mathlib has a two-tier system, of reviewers and maintainers. Maintainers have the final say, but reviewers support this by sharing the reviewer load. In practice, 1/3 PRs gets approved by a review before a maintainer merges it.
  • (5) is not about using Python or shell scripts. (I presume it refers to the implementation of the review dashboard.) By the way, that section is outdated; the dashboard has been rewritten by Bryan Gin-ge Chen.

@Michael Rothgang , I'm sorry for the bad communication in the message above (I meant the message as a quick update since i hadn't given any since few days, I should have clarified that :sweat_smile: )
let me provide the correct details, thanks for taking time to give the feedback :

(3): Yes, even in PhysLib, the final merge happens only after approval from the maintainer, what I wanted to convey was 1/3rd of all such merges in mathlib happened in a fashion where the maintainers' only intervention was to approve the final merge.
(5): I was quoting the second last para on page 15 under section 7.2. (The two green highlights):

Thanks for mentioning the update, will take into account!
Note that (3) is still slightly off --- the paper does not say what you're thinking :-)

I mentioned this elsewhere somewhere but can't find it now - it would be nice to be able to encode future API plans directly in the Lean files, to form a sort of Physlib-suitable blueprint of areas of future work.

Hi! I'm working on the queueboard now with the mathlib initiative. If you have questions about the queueboard feel free to ping me.
Need feedback: Mathlib autolabel.lean excludes CI, IMO and dependency-bump folders from assignment, what are the equivalents in physlib ? (Asking now since it would anyways come up during PR review)
If I understand the question I think the equivalent would be the ./scripts file? But am not sure I totally understand.

Shlok Vaibhav said:

Need feedback: Mathlib autolabel.lean excludes CI, IMO and dependency-bump folders from assignment, what are the equivalents in physlib ? (Asking now since it would anyways come up during PR review)

I don't really understand your question.

  • autolabel.sh does add the CI label (you seem to claim otherwise)
  • CI, IMO and dependency-bump are PR labels, not folders
  • the autolabel script is for adding "area" labels to PRs, not for assigning reviewers

I'm sorry, realized I asked incorrect question, here's what I would ask:

Mathlib has two label strings - those which start with t- - these are the subject topics in mathlib like Algebra etc.
I have made analogous labels in PhysLib. These labels exhuastively covered the Mathlib folder inside mathlib repo

Then there are three labels in mathlib - CI, IMO and dependency-bump that don't start with t- label as they are not topic folders but map to scripts, and folders like archive/IMO (Which refers to olympiad?).

So the coverage of autolabel.lean in mathlib repo is - entire mathlib folder + some infrastructure folders covered by the three labels, CI, IMO and dependency-bump. However the mathlib repo itself is not exhaustively covered by these labels.

So my question is: for Physlib, apart from the exhuastive coverge of Physlib and QuantumInfo folders, what are some equivalents of CI, IMO kind of labels that cover more folders containing scripts etc (while entire repo is still not exhaustively covered)??
Got it! We could probably have a autolabelling for PhyslibAlpha, dependency bumps and scripts (though for the latter two we would need new labels) - if this seems good I can make said labels.
Thanks, i will include these as well and put some labels that can be changed while review.

It's probably worth the enforced clarity to use CODEOWNERS, or even better, whatever mathlib is doing. It's an intuitive idea for what is essentially a human and labor organizational problem, for which there are never easy or complete solutions.

I created an issue about the current linting infrastructure before realizing it's probably bigger than just physlib. Any suggestions would be appreciated. If it's a matter of just improving the robustness of the python code, I can certainly do that, but still argue it's better for lean to do this natively.

As a follow up to this: I think one thing which would be in addition helpful here is the following:

  • Automatically putting the ready-to-merge label on a PR which has an approving review and passes all the CI.

Also would be nice to

  • Remove awaiting-author tag automatically when the author makes a change to a PR.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Also would be nice to

  • Remove awaiting-author tag automatically when the author makes a change to a PR.

As a mathlib author, I disagree with that one. It's not uncommon for me to address some review comments, but not all of them. I agree that this can be a trap new contributors fall into, though --- I'd rather teach them to comment -awaiting-authorwhen it's ready again. (Rust has a @rustbot ready command, which is nicely self-explanatory. It wouldn't be hard to add a similar variant here.)

Ok, I think this is fair. I had not thought of this. Maybe an alternative is that if the awaiting-author tag is put on someone's PR, then an automatic comment is sent saying something like: 

Your PR has been tagged with `awaiting-author`, please address any comments. Once done please comment with `-awaiting-author` to remove this tag, and ensure the review process works smoothly.

For contextual documentation of the awaiting-authorand other flag expectations, you could also add a comment block in the PR template. It could even just point to another page with this information as well. Right now the PR template is empty.
Ah this is not a bad idea - alternatively since we are already including a comment via a workflow on PRs, it can be added to that. I've done this here Physlib#1205 as a temporary solution.

Maybe just indicate what is taken from Mathlib would help here.

Almost everything is copied verbatim from mathlib file, except name changes and additional changes to incorporate quantuminfo folder, As a specific doubt I have is line 228-238 in my file, a function that finds the labels for a given filepath:

def getMatchingLabels (files : Array FilePath) : Array Label :=
  let applicable := physlibLabels.filter fun label ↦
    -- first exclude all files the label excludes,
    -- then see if any file remains included by the label
    let data := physlibLabelData label
    let notExcludedFiles := files.filter fun file ↦
      data.exclusions.all (!·.isPrefixOf file)
    data.dirs.any (fun dir ↦ notExcludedFiles.any (dir.isPrefixOf ·))
  -- return sorted list of labels
  applicable |>.qsort (·.toString < ·.toString)

In a PR review, we need to understand and become satisfied with the correctness of this code. How do we do this here:
A. Since it's copied verbatim from mathlib, it wont be reviewed? (Seems unlikely answer)
B. I can give an additional line-by-line explanation in a separete document to show that the code was understood by me and the PR reviewer can use those explanations to review the code correctness? (For this attached example, the additional file will have a line-by-line explanation of what each line in this borrowed code is doing)

How have previous portings from mathlib been handled?

Is it worth including the line-by-line explanation directly in the code itself? I understand for a normal programming language this would not be convention, but here it might be worth it, as there is a gap between knowing Lean and knowing meta-programming in Lean.

I don't think we have had previous ports from Mathlib bin the recent past - I think most of the ones we have come from the very early stages of the project, where things were different.
Yes, I can do that before making the PR
